screens.title: Designing for Disaster Recovery in Azure Data Engineering
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to design disaster recovery for core Azure data engineering services so business operations can continue when a region fails. We will clarify the difference between high availability and disaster recovery, and why RTO and RPO drive your design choices. You will see concrete strategies for Azure S Q L Database, Synapse Analytics, ADLS Gen2, Data Factory, and Databricks, and understand how Azure Backup and Azure Site Recovery fit into a comprehensive plan. I will also guide you through a conceptual geo-restore for a Synapse dedicated S Q L pool and a practical approach to protect Azure Data Factory metadata using Git integration. By the end you'll be able to choose replication and backup options that balance cost, complexity, and acceptable data loss, and you'll know the common mistakes to avoid. Think now about a dataset you are responsible for: what recovery time and data loss would be acceptable if a region became unavailable?

Designing for Disaster Recovery
Prepare cross-region plans for databases, storage, pipelines, and compute so your data platform survives a regional outage.

screens.title: HA vs DR and the RTO / RPO timeline
screens.narratorSegment: Start by separating two common but different goals. High availability focuses on minimizing disruption inside a single region. It uses redundancy, replicas, and failover within the same region to keep services running during localized faults. Disaster recovery, by contrast, prepares for region-wide loss and often requires cross‑region replication and redeployment. Two metrics make these choices concrete: Recovery Time Objective, the maximum acceptable duration of downtime after a disaster, and Recovery Point Objective, the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. For example, if your RTO is thirty minutes you will pick solutions that enable fast failover or warm standby; if your RPO is near zero you need continuous synchronous replication or active geo-replication. A common misconception is to assume HA always covers DR—HA may not survive a full region outage. In practice you draw a timeline that places backups, replication frequency, and failover activities along the RPO/RTO axis. Your takeaway: define acceptable RTO and RPO first, then choose patterns—backups for long RTO/RPO, geo-replication or continuous replication for short RTO/RPO. What RTO and RPO would your team define for a critical pipeline?

keyIdea.title: Define before you design
keyIdea.text: RTO and RPO should be established up front; they determine whether you use backups, asynchronous replication, or continuous geo-replication.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › HA vs DR & RTO/RPO
Concept: HA versus DR
HA tackles localized failures; DR prepares for regional outages and requires cross-region replication or redeployment.
Definition
RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service. RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
Concrete example
If your RPO is five minutes, asynchronous replication like GRS may not suffice; you need near-continuous replication or application-level strategies to reduce data loss.
Misconception
Assuming HA equals DR. HA does not protect against a whole-region failure, which is the focus of DR planning.
Key Takeaway

Set RTO and RPO first; then select backups, asynchronous replication, or continuous geo-replication to meet those targets.

RTO / RPO Timeline
Timeline (short to long)
Near zero RPO
Continuous replication, active geo-replication
Minutes RPO
Frequent differential or log shipping strategies
Hours or more
Backups and geo-restore from snapshots
Check your understanding
Which combination of replication and backup would you choose for an RTO of 1 hour and RPO of 30 minutes? Think about replication frequency and restore steps.

screens.title: Azure SQL Database — Active geo-replication and failover groups
screens.narratorSegment: Azure S Q L Database supports cross-region Disaster Recovery through Active Geo-Replication and Auto-Failover Groups. Active geo-replication continuously replicates changes from a primary database to one or more readable secondary databases in another region. This allows you to switch users to the secondary in a disaster, often with manual or automated failover depending on how you configure failover groups. A concrete example: you have a primary in Region A and a secondary in Region B; with active geo-replication the secondary stays nearly up to date and can be made primary in case Region A fails. A common misconception is expecting no data loss; because replication can be asynchronous, some transactions may not reach the secondary before a region failure, so RPO is not guaranteed to be zero. When using auto-failover groups you can automate failover for multiple databases and manage DNS updates, but you still need to plan connection string changes or DNS TTLs because a failover may require pointing clients to a new server endpoint. Key takeaway: Active geo-replication and failover groups provide a practical DR path for managed S Q L, but confirm your RTO and RPO expectations before relying on them.

keyIdea.title: SQL DR pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Active Geo-Replication for near-continuous cross-region copies and Auto-Failover Groups to orchestrate database-level failover.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › Azure SQL DR
Active Geo-Replication
Continuously replicate to readable secondaries in another region to enable manual or orchestrated failover.
How it works
Transactions are sent to a secondary; the secondary can be promoted to primary during recovery.
Example
Primary in Region A, secondary in Region B. Use failover group for coordinated failover and DNS management.
Misconception
Expect asynchronous replication to be perfect. In a sudden regional failure, some committed transactions may not have arrived at the secondary.
Architecture
Primary DB
Handles read/write workload and sends transaction log data to secondaries.
Secondary DB
Readable replica in a different region that can be promoted during DR.
Check your understanding
If an application requires zero data loss, would active geo-replication alone be sufficient? Consider replication mode and possible trade-offs.
Key Takeaway

Active geo-replication plus failover groups gives cross-region continuity, but validate RPO expectations for your workload.

screens.title: Automated backups, point-in-time restore, and long-term retention
screens.narratorSegment: Backups are the foundation of many DR strategies. Azure S Q L Database provides automated full, differential, and transaction log backups that are stored in geo-redundant storage; you can use point-in-time restore to recover to any backup within the retention period. For long-term retention you can configure backups to be stored in Azure Blob Storage for up to ten years. Azure Synapse dedicated S Q L pools also take snapshots automatically throughout the day and store them in your ADLS Gen2 account; those snapshots are geo-redundant and you can perform a geo-restore to create a new S Q L pool in another region from those snapshots. An important example: if you discover data corruption introduced hours ago, point-in-time restore lets you roll back to a time before the corruption. A misconception is relying solely on snapshots without planning for connection string updates and server targets; geo-restore creates a new S Q L pool in a new region, so you must update endpoints. The key takeaway: backups and snapshots give you flexible recovery points and long-term retention, but recovery procedures must include endpoint and DNS planning so applications reconnect smoothly.

keyIdea.title: Backups are essential
keyIdea.text: Automated backups and snapshots provide recoverable points; long-term retention supports compliance while geo-restore enables cross-region recovery.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › Backups & Restore
Automated Backups & PITR
Full, differential, and log backups enable point-in-time restores within retention windows.
{
  "backupTypes": ["full","diff","log"],
  "retentionDays": 35,
  "geoRedundant": true
}
Example
Use point-in-time restore to recover a database to a time before an accidental data change or corruption.
Geo-restore for Synapse
Synapse dedicated SQL pools use geo-redundant snapshots stored in ADLS Gen2. A geo-restore creates a new SQL pool in another region from these snapshots.
Misconception
Assuming geo-restore preserves the same server and endpoint. Geo-restore creates a new pool; you must update connection strings or DNS entries.
Key Takeaway

Backups and snapshots provide the recovery points you need; include endpoint and configuration updates in your recovery runbook.

screens.title: Serverless SQL pools and ADLS Gen2 — stateless compute, resilient storage
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless S Q L pools separate compute from storage: the compute is stateless and queries data where it lives, typically in ADLS Gen2. This means disaster recovery for serverless S Q L primarily depends on the durability and replication of the underlying storage rather than the compute itself. If your ADLS Gen2 account is configured with geo-redundant options, the storage can be recovered or read from another region, while compute is redeployed without preserving local state. A concrete example: if a region fails, you recreate your serverless compute in the secondary region and point it at the geo-replicated ADLS Gen2 account or the secondary storage endpoint. A common mistake is expecting the serverless compute instance to be automatically available in the secondary region; compute is stateless and must be reprovisioned. The takeaway: protect data first by selecting appropriate ADLS Gen2 replication, then plan rapid reprovisioning of serverless compute so queries can resume quickly. Serverless SQL pools and ADLS Gen2 — stateless compute, resilient storage means protect adls gen2 with geo-redundant options; reprovision serverless compute in the dr region to resume queries.. In practical terms, why serverless compute relies on adls gen2 replication for dr. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Protect ADLS Gen2 with geo-redundant options; reprovision serverless compute in the DR region to resume queries.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › Serverless SQL & ADLS Gen2
Serverless compute is stateless
Recovery focuses on the underlying ADLS Gen2 storage, which must be geo-replicated for cross-region DR.
Concrete scenario
After a regional outage, reprovision serverless compute in the DR region and point it to the geo-replicated ADLS Gen2 endpoint to resume queries.
Common mistake
Expecting compute to automatically exist in the secondary region. Plan for reprovisioning as part of your runbook.
Key Takeaway

Protect the storage layer with appropriate replication; treat compute as disposable and automatable for faster recovery.

Quick checklist
  • Confirm ADLS Gen2 uses GRS/GZRS or custom replication for your RPO needs.
  • Have IaC templates or automation to reprovision serverless SQL compute.
  • Validate access and identity mappings after reprovisioning.

screens.title: ADLS Gen2 replication: GRS, GZRS, and read-access options
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 offers replication tiers that affect durability and cross-region access. Geo-Redundant Storage (GRS) asynchronously replicates data to a secondary paired region. Geo-Zone-Redundant Storage (GZRS) adds zone redundancy in the primary region and also replicates to a secondary region. Read-Access variants—RA-GRS and RA-GZRS—allow you to read from the secondary region before initiating a full failover, which can be useful for DR drills or read-only analytics when the primary is unavailable. A concrete example: if your analytics job can run with slightly stale data during an outage, RA-GRS lets you continue reads from the secondary while you plan a full failover. A misconception to avoid is treating asynchronous replication as continuous guarantee; because replication is asynchronous, the RPO is not zero and some recent writes may be lost during failover. For workloads that require a lower RPO than GRS provides, consider explicit cross-region copies with Azure Data Factory or AzCopy at a higher frequency. Key takeaway: pick the replication tier based on whether you need read access in the secondary region and how much data loss is acceptable.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › ADLS Gen2 Replication
Replication options
Compare GRS, GZRS, and read-access variants for cross-region durability and availability.
GRS
Asynchronous replication to a secondary paired region. Useful for simple geo-protection.
GZRS
Zone-redundant in primary region plus asynchronous replication to a secondary region for higher durability.
RA-GRS / RA-GZRS
Read access to the secondary region before failover, useful for analytics during outages.
Custom copies
Use ADF or AzCopy to copy critical data at higher frequency when GRS's async replication RPO is insufficient.
Check your understanding
If you need readable data in the secondary region immediately during an outage, which storage option would you select and why?
Decision guide
  • Choose GZRS for higher durability across zones.
  • Choose RA variants when read access in the secondary region matters.
  • Use custom replication for lower RPO than asynchronous replication provides.

screens.title: Custom cross-region replication with ADF and AzCopy
screens.narratorSegment: When your RPO requirement is lower than the asynchronous replication window, a common approach is to implement explicit cross-region copies. Tools like Azure Data Factory or AzCopy can copy data to a secondary ADLS Gen2 account at a controlled frequency. For example, configure an ADF pipeline that runs hourly or every few minutes to copy changed files to the DR account. This reduces potential data loss compared to relying solely on GRS/GZRS asynchronous replication. A concrete example: schedule a Data Factory pipeline to copy newly landed parquet files every five minutes into a secondary account. A misconception is assuming that increasing copy frequency eliminates all risk—there is still a window between copies, and cost and complexity rise with frequency. Also, ensure you replicate metadata like ACLs and partition layouts so the secondary copy is usable. The takeaway: explicit, scheduled copying gives you tighter control over RPO at the cost of bandwidth and operational complexity; use it where stricter RPOs are required. Custom cross-region replication with ADF and AzCopy means use adf or azcopy to replicate data at controlled intervals when storage replication's rpo is insufficient.. In practical terms, when asynchronous storage replication doesn't meet your rpo, use active copying. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › Custom Replication
ADF or AzCopy for tighter RPO
Schedule frequent, controlled copies to a secondary ADLS Gen2 account to reduce data loss risk.
Example
An ADF pipeline copies new parquet files every five minutes into a secondary account to lower RPO.
Operational notes
Account for costs, bandwidth, and the need to preserve ACLs and partition metadata during copies.
Misconception
Higher frequency eliminates risk. It reduces it, but there's still a window and higher operational cost.
Implementation checklist
  • Identify files or partitions to replicate.
  • Design an ADF pipeline or AzCopy schedule and monitor job success.
  • Replicate ACLs and partitioning metadata where needed.

screens.title: Azure Data Factory DR: Git integration and SHIR strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Data Factory is a globally distributed service, but its metadata—pipelines, datasets, linked services, and triggers—resides in a single region. To protect that metadata you should integrate ADF with Git (Azure DevOps Git or GitHub). When configured, your pipelines and configurations are stored as JSON ARM templates in the repository. In a disaster you can provision a new ADF instance in another region and connect it to the same Git repository to redeploy metadata, achieving a low RPO for configuration. For connectivity, Self-Hosted Integration Runtimes (SHIRs) are critical: deploy SHIRs in both primary and secondary regions or have an automated plan to stand up new SHIRs in the DR region. screens.title: Azure Databricks DR: IaC, Git, metastore and secrets
screens.narratorSegment: Databricks has no built-in cross-region workspace replication, so your DR strategy must cover workspace configuration, notebooks, underlying data, metastores, and secrets. The common approach is Infrastructure as Code to define the workspace, and Git integration for notebooks and libraries. In a disaster you deploy a new workspace in the DR region using your IaC templates and restore notebooks and libraries from the Git repository. For data, rely on ADLS Gen2 replication or use ADF to copy data to a secondary account. If you use an external Hive metastore, ensure that metastore is geo-replicated—often by using geo-replicated Azure S Q L Database—to maintain table metadata. Secrets in Key Vault must be replicated to the secondary region so jobs can access credentials. A concrete example: keep notebooks in Databricks Repos backed by Git and have an ARM or Terraform template to recreate workspace networking and cluster policies. A common mistake is overlooking secrets and metastores during tests; without them, redeployed clusters cannot access data or execute jobs. The takeaway: treat Databricks as a composition of components—IaC for the workspace, Git for code, replicated storage for data, and replicated metastore and secrets for full recoverability.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to design disaster recovery for core Azure data engineering services so business operations can continue when a region fails. We will clarify the difference between high availability and disaster recovery, and why RTO and RPO drive your design choices. You will see concrete strategies for Azure S Q L Database, Synapse Analytics, ADLS Gen2, Data Factory, and Databricks, and understand how Azure Backup and Azure Site Recovery fit into a comprehensive plan. I will also guide you through a conceptual geo-restore for a Synapse dedicated S Q L pool and a practical approach to protect Azure Data Factory metadata using Git integration. By the end you'll be able to choose replication and backup options that balance cost, complexity, and acceptable data loss, and you'll know the common mistakes to avoid. Think now about a dataset you are responsible for: what recovery time and data loss would be acceptable if a region became unavailable?

By the end of this chapter you will distinguish high availability from disaster recovery and use RTO and RPO to make design decisions. You will implement backup and restore approaches for Azure S Q L Database and Azure Synapse Analytics, including point-in-time restores and geo-restore procedures. You will design cross-region replication for ADLS Gen2 using GRS and GZRS, and plan read-access options for failover scenarios. You will also develop a DR plan for Azure Data Factory and Databricks by using Git integration, Infrastructure as Code, and replication of external metadata. Finally, you will integrate Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup where VMs or file shares are part of your data platform. Each objective emphasizes why the skill matters, shows a practical example, and points to a verification milestone so you can confirm competency.

This second objectives slide explains how to verify your disaster recovery skills. You will practice a conceptual geo-restore for a Synapse dedicated S Q L pool and configure Azure Data Factory to use Git so your metadata is versioned and redeployable. You will design a replication plan for ADLS Gen2 and simulate read-access scenarios with RA-GRS or RA-GZRS to shorten your recovery window. For Databricks, you will prepare an IaC template and confirm notebooks and libraries are stored in a Git repository. Finally, you will plan tests and drills so you regularly validate RTO and RPO assumptions. Each verification step focuses on a measurable milestone: successful restore simulation, repository import, or redeployment of resources from IaC. These checkpoints confirm your design meets the business requirements you defined earlier. Learning Objectives — Skills and Verification means use drills, repository imports, and iac redeployments as measurable milestones to confirm your dr strategy meets rto and rpo goals.. In practical terms, how to validate competency and apply dr patterns. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Start by separating two common but different goals. High availability focuses on minimizing disruption inside a single region. It uses redundancy, replicas, and failover within the same region to keep services running during localized faults. Disaster recovery, by contrast, prepares for region-wide loss and often requires cross‑region replication and redeployment. Two metrics make these choices concrete: Recovery Time Objective, the maximum acceptable duration of downtime after a disaster, and Recovery Point Objective, the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. For example, if your RTO is thirty minutes you will pick solutions that enable fast failover or warm standby; if your RPO is near zero you need continuous synchronous replication or active geo-replication. A common misconception is to assume HA always covers DR—HA may not survive a full region outage. In practice you draw a timeline that places backups, replication frequency, and failover activities along the RPO/RTO axis. Your takeaway: define acceptable RTO and RPO first, then choose patterns—backups for long RTO/RPO, geo-replication or continuous replication for short RTO/RPO. What RTO and RPO would your team define for a critical pipeline?

Azure S Q L Database supports cross-region Disaster Recovery through Active Geo-Replication and Auto-Failover Groups. Active geo-replication continuously replicates changes from a primary database to one or more readable secondary databases in another region. This allows you to switch users to the secondary in a disaster, often with manual or automated failover depending on how you configure failover groups. A concrete example: you have a primary in Region A and a secondary in Region B; with active geo-replication the secondary stays nearly up to date and can be made primary in case Region A fails. A common misconception is expecting no data loss; because replication can be asynchronous, some transactions may not reach the secondary before a region failure, so RPO is not guaranteed to be zero. When using auto-failover groups you can automate failover for multiple databases and manage DNS updates, but you still need to plan connection string changes or DNS TTLs because a failover may require pointing clients to a new server endpoint. Key takeaway: Active geo-replication and failover groups provide a practical DR path for managed S Q L, but confirm your RTO and RPO expectations before relying on them.

Backups are the foundation of many DR strategies. Azure S Q L Database provides automated full, differential, and transaction log backups that are stored in geo-redundant storage; you can use point-in-time restore to recover to any backup within the retention period. For long-term retention you can configure backups to be stored in Azure Blob Storage for up to ten years. Azure Synapse dedicated S Q L pools also take snapshots automatically throughout the day and store them in your ADLS Gen2 account; those snapshots are geo-redundant and you can perform a geo-restore to create a new S Q L pool in another region from those snapshots. An important example: if you discover data corruption introduced hours ago, point-in-time restore lets you roll back to a time before the corruption. A misconception is relying solely on snapshots without planning for connection string updates and server targets; geo-restore creates a new S Q L pool in a new region, so you must update endpoints. The key takeaway: backups and snapshots give you flexible recovery points and long-term retention, but recovery procedures must include endpoint and DNS planning so applications reconnect smoothly.

Serverless S Q L pools separate compute from storage: the compute is stateless and queries data where it lives, typically in ADLS Gen2. This means disaster recovery for serverless S Q L primarily depends on the durability and replication of the underlying storage rather than the compute itself. If your ADLS Gen2 account is configured with geo-redundant options, the storage can be recovered or read from another region, while compute is redeployed without preserving local state. A concrete example: if a region fails, you recreate your serverless compute in the secondary region and point it at the geo-replicated ADLS Gen2 account or the secondary storage endpoint. A common mistake is expecting the serverless compute instance to be automatically available in the secondary region; compute is stateless and must be reprovisioned. The takeaway: protect data first by selecting appropriate ADLS Gen2 replication, then plan rapid reprovisioning of serverless compute so queries can resume quickly. Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 offers replication tiers that affect durability and cross-region access. Geo-Redundant Storage (GRS) asynchronously replicates data to a secondary paired region. Geo-Zone-Redundant Storage (GZRS) adds zone redundancy in the primary region and also replicates to a secondary region. Read-Access variants—RA-GRS and RA-GZRS—allow you to read from the secondary region before initiating a full failover, which can be useful for DR drills or read-only analytics when the primary is unavailable. A concrete example: if your analytics job can run with slightly stale data during an outage, RA-GRS lets you continue reads from the secondary while you plan a full failover. A misconception to avoid is treating asynchronous replication as continuous guarantee; because replication is asynchronous, the RPO is not zero and some recent writes may be lost during failover. For workloads that require a lower RPO than GRS provides, consider explicit cross-region copies with Azure Data Factory or AzCopy at a higher frequency. Key takeaway: pick the replication tier based on whether you need read access in the secondary region and how much data loss is acceptable.

When your RPO requirement is lower than the asynchronous replication window, a common approach is to implement explicit cross-region copies. Tools like Azure Data Factory or AzCopy can copy data to a secondary ADLS Gen2 account at a controlled frequency. For example, configure an ADF pipeline that runs hourly or every few minutes to copy changed files to the DR account. A misconception is assuming that increasing copy frequency eliminates all risk—there is still a window between copies, and cost and complexity rise with frequency. Also, ensure you replicate metadata like ACLs and partition layouts so the secondary copy is usable. The takeaway: explicit, scheduled copying gives you tighter control over RPO at the cost of bandwidth and operational complexity; use it where stricter RPOs are required.
